svg.text: Uncertainty, significant figures, precision and accuracy

g.text: 40 cm

svg.text: book: one edge at 10.0 cm, the other at 33.5 cm

g.text: a metre rule graduated in millimetres has an absolute uncertainty of one smallest division, 1 mm
the true length lies between 23.4 cm and 23.6 cm
fractional uncertainty = absolute uncertainty / measured value
percentage uncertainty = (absolute uncertainty / measured value) x 100

svg.text: digital scale: estimate one digit beyond what is certain; a last digit that fluctuates
by more than about 2 is not really significant

g.text: reading
least count
fractional
percentage
25.5 cm, metre rule
0.1 cm
0.45 cm, Vernier callipers
precision: set by the instrument; the smaller the least
count (absolute uncertainty), the more precise the measurement
accuracy: closeness to the exact or accepted value; the
smaller the fractional or percentage uncertainty, the more
accurate the measurement
so 25.5 cm is less precise but more accurate; 0.45 cm is
more precise but less accurate: a small quantity needs a
more precise instrument (screw gauge, 0.001 cm)

svg.text: Significant figures (1.4): the digits of a measurement we feel reasonably sure about

g.text: counting: all digits 1 to 9 count; a zero between significant figures counts; zeros to the left do not
(0.00467, 02.59); zeros to the right count in a decimal fraction (3.570, 7.4000); in an integer such as
8,000 kg they depend on the least count: 8.000 x 10^3 kg (1 kg) has four, 8.00 x 10^3 kg (10 kg) has three;
in scientific notation the figures other than the power of ten count: 8.70 x 10^4 kg has three
multiplying or dividing: keep no more significant figures than the least accurate factor
rounding: first dropped digit below 5, keep; above 5, add one; exactly 5, add one if the kept
adding or subtracting: keep the smallest number of decimal places, not of significant figures
same object, two balances: electronic 3.145 +/- 0.001 g, lever 3.1 +/- 0.1 g; 3.145 g shows the better instrument
limitation: significant figures cover only the scale-reading uncertainty; personal and hidden systematic
errors can make the total uncertainty larger than the figures suggest
addition or subtraction: same precision
(decimal places)
multiplication or division: same accuracy
(number of significant figures)
uncertainty = mean deviation from the
average value
least count of the timing device divided
by the number of oscillations
precision: less absolute uncertainty
accuracy: less percentage uncertainty
we can never make an exact measurement
